title: TS: How well do we enable people to live fully until they die?
description:
Research into Rehabilitation in Palliative Care.

1) What we mean by 'Living fully until you die' and why it matters is appraised through diverse lenses from person to population:
- ‘What matters most’: a research synthesis on priorities of people living with palliative diagnoses - invites audience reflection
- ‘The disability pandemic’: an interrogation of the impact of cancer, advanced chronic illness, multimorbidity, ageing and frailty on function, independence, care needs and costs - sets the context for rehabilitation as a solution.
2) Cutting-edge research and practice examples from high, middle and low-income countries illustrate the value of rehabilitation in palliative care and how to integrate it to enable people to live fully until they die:
- ‘Rehabilitation is everybody’s business’: towards a consensus definition and shared understanding- ‘From contradiction to evidence-based best practice’: history and literature- ‘A radical culture shift’ an integrated rehabilitative, palliative and geriatric approach for older people living with frailty.

Aim and learning objectives:

To challenge participants to consider how well they enable people with advanced, serious illness, old age or frailty to live fully until they die – critically interrogating what we mean by this founding aspiration of palliative care and how it is realised and evaluated in practice and research.
To expand participants' understanding of rehabilitation in palliative care as an integrated approach to enable people to live fully until they die through a compelling synthesis of research, innovative examples, international recommendations and an interactive expert panel discussion.

title: EAPC groups: Maximising the inclusivity of the public health approach to bereavement
description:
This session focuses on the research-based public health model for bereavement care. It poses questions for discussion on the translation of bereavement research into policy and practice, and more specifically, on implications for bereavement care for minoritised communities, including cultural and faith-based communities, those in prisons, the LGBTQI community, and people who are homeless. 
Session one is an initial overview of the public health model for bereavement care, compassionate communities and associated evidence. Session two is a data-driven case study on how the public health model is implemented in a large urban hospital setting, and session three outlines policy and practice implementation examples on how bereavement care is managed and rolled out through a range of marginalised settings. 
Three EAPC taskforces/reference groups will be represented: the Bereavement Taskforce, the Social Work Taskforce and the EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. 
Session aim: 
To explore a critical approach to the implementation of the public health bereavement model: integrating bereavement knowledge into practice for the benefit of all communities.  
Learning objectives:
• Integrate bereavement approaches across relevant task forces and reference groups at EAPC, including the Bereavement Taskforce, the Social Work Taskforce and the EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. 
• Identify the evidence base for an inclusive public health approach to bereavement care  
• Appraise the challenges and opportunities for translating bereavement research evidence into practice for all communities, including seldom heard and minority groups

Speakers:

Prof Samar Aoun, Perron Institute Research Chair in Palliative Care, The University of Western Australia.     EAPC Public Health and Palliative Care Reference Group. PRE-REC
Dr Steve Marshall, King’s College Hospital and King’s College London EAPC Social Work Taskforce 
Prof Audrey Roulston, Queen's University Belfast, Co-Chair EAPC Social Work Taskforce 
Irene Murphy and Orla Keegan, Co-Chairs EAPC Bereavement Taskforce

title: TS: Towards gold-standard methods in paediatric palliative care research, sharing knowledge, assessing challenges and opportunities.
description:
Research into Paediatric Palliative Care.

Effective delivery and adequate resourcing of healthcare rely on high-quality evidence to drive decisions. To date, PPC research has largely comprised small cohort studies (case studies, chart reviews, etc.).
Session aim:Explore opportunities and challenges in applying best-practice research methods to PPC research, through knowledge sharing across multiple disciplines, thereby strengthening the evidence base on which PPC delivery, resourcing, and planning decisions are made.

Learning objectives:Developing understanding and awareness of:-	opportunities for engaging with children and families in research-	real/perceived challenges in applying robust evaluation techniques in PPC (e.g., randomised controlled trials)-	methods for population-level planning of PPC.
The session will comprise three short presentations followed by structured discussion time.
Presentation 1 will focus on the increasingly vital role of Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) in health services research, specifically highlighting the engagement of children and young people (CYP). Prof Veronica Lambert will chart the evidence on CYP involvement as active PPI contributors across all stages of the PPC research cycle. 
Presentation 2 will examine real/perceived challenges to conducting randomised controlled trials and other robust evaluation techniques in PPC research. Prof Lorna Fraser will demonstrate the availability of core building blocks required for measuring effectiveness and cost effectiveness in PPC and discuss challenges and opportunities for advancing methods further.
Presentation 3 will highlight recent learnings from national level analysis on planning for PPC. Dr Samantha Smith will discuss challenges in defining need for PPC at a population-level, incorporating markers of complexity and applicability of methods to different data sources.

title: EAPC Partnered Research
description:
Chaired by Patricia White and Tamara Radojicic (Pal-Cycles)
Panel 1: Recruitment, equity and inclusion in trials
This panel will explore how equity, inclusion and diversity can be embedded across study design, consortium governance, implementation and dissemination, with attention to structural inequities in access, inclusive recruitment, culturally and linguistically appropriate methods, and equitable partnership models. The session will highlight practical strategies and measurable indicators.
Panellists: Lise Nottleman (INSPIRE), Everlien de Graaf (RAPHAEL), Manuel Luís Vila Capelas (Pal-Cycles), Nicola Cornally (In Touch) 

Panel 2: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence in palliative care research 
This panel will examine how AI can be responsibly integrated into research projects to enhance communication training, personalise care planning, support clinical decision-making, and generate real-world evidence, while addressing risks such as algorithmic bias, data governance, and digital exclusion.
Panellists: Izidor Mlakar (AI4HOPE), Alexander Varjord (INSPIRE), Jan Hrdlička (VR Talks), Carsten Klein

title: EAPC Groups: Palliative oxygen therapy: preliminary guidelines and reconsideration within the palliative care continuum
description:
This session is planned to discuss clinical guidelines regarding palliative oxygen therapy. These guidelines are generated by the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Oxygen Therapy and regard POT definition, outcome measures follow up and regimens. This task force was developed in recognition of the need to support the use of palliative oxygen therapy. Currently, its use is limited due to a lack of a consensual definition, due to unclear eligibility, limited evidence supporting various regimens (low flow versus high flow therapy) and the lack of validated outcome measures. We established several working groups within this Task Force and tried to gather and analyse the existing evidence on the above mentioned issues. Some of the evidence is generated via systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature, and some other is generated based on consensus elicited via the Delphi procedure. For both categories, it would be very useful to have an interactive exchange of opinions before wrapping everything up and drafting the clinical guideline paper.

Questions and learning objectives:  
How should palliative oxygen therapy be defined? 
Should low-flow oxygen therapy be used to improve symptoms in people with chronic serious illness who do not meet the criteria for LTOT? 
Should high-flow oxygen therapy be used to improve symptoms in people with chronic serious illness who do not meet the criteria for LTOT? 
What are the eligibility criteria for palliative oxygen therapy? 
How should palliative oxygen therapy be administered and followed up? 

Speakers:

Prof Sabina Antoniu, University of Medicine and Pharmacy Grigore T Popa Iasi, Romania 
Prof Magnus Ekström, Lund University, Sweden

Dr Slavica Kochovska, Flinders University Adelaide, Australia
Dr Filip Bjorklund, Lund University, Sweden

All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Oxygen Therapy.

title: TS: Methodological approaches to research into requests for assisted dying: added value & challenges
description:
Research into Requests for Assisted Dying.

In this themed session, participants will engage with diverse research on requests for assisted dying in palliative care, conducted using distinct methodologies and situated in different countries and contexts. The main emphasis will be on the employed methodologies, examining the novelty and added value of each approach in uncovering relevant insights, as well as the challenges and pitfalls they present in data collection and analysis. Through a rich and in-depth group interaction process, participants will leave the session with a range of recommendations for further research and practice.

Content of the session:- Short introduction to the session
- Three concise presentations on research into requests for assisted dying, which, next to sharing the main findings, will focus on the methodologies used, their added value, and the complexities encountered. Each contribution will centre on a distinct methodological approach:
1) international comparative research;
2) qualitative ethnographic approaches;
3) consensus-building methods
- a moderated group discussion on issues related to doing research on assisted dying (and its relationship to palliative care).

title: EAPC Partnered Research
description:
Chaired by Fódhla Ní Chéileachair (EAPC) and Everlien de Graaf (RAPHAEL)
Panel 3: Issues with implementation
This panel will explore barriers such as regulatory variation, workforce capacity, cultural differences, integration into routine care, sustainability beyond project funding, and uneven adoption across countries. The session will identify practical strategies from implementation science to enhance scalability, long-term impact, and real-world uptake of palliative care innovations across Europe.
Panellists: Elias Lundereng (MyPath), Lieve van den Block (EuNavigate), Sergi Navaro (PALLIAKID), Suzanne Timmons (IN TOUCH and AI4Hope)
Panel 4: Moving research into practice
This panel will examine the gap between evidence generation and real-world adoption, exploring knowledge translation strategies, stakeholder engagement and sustainable service integration across diverse European health systems. The session will highlight practical models and success factors that enable research findings to influence clinical practice and organisational change at scale.
Panellists: Katrine Rolid (EUonQOL, JANE2), Roman Rolke (RAPHAEL), Ulf Bremberg (PsyPal), Jo Bayly (INSPIRE)

title: EAPC Groups: Palliative Care Meets Emergency Medical Services. An International Call to Action
description:
The integration of palliative care into out-of-hospital emergency services is gaining momentum worldwide. People with life-limiting illnesses often face acute medical emergencies, which, in the absence of clear communication and structural pathways, may lead to distressing overtreatment from emergency care workers. This session presents experiences from South Africa, Australia and Germany on systematically strengthening palliative care within EMS — from provider and patient surveys to concrete implementation concepts, in addition to an overview of the state of palliative paramedicine affairs globally. Building on these insights, a proposal for a European White Paper will be introduced. The session aims to foster international exchange and develop joint recommendations for improving palliative care in EMS across Europe and further abroad.

The aims and learning objectives:

 - Understand the unique role of Emergency Medical Services (EMS) in delivering palliative care.  
 - Explore how integrating palliative care benefits EMS, palliative care services, patient outcomes and the broader healthcare system, through a global systems lens. 
 - Learn from international models, including South Africa (low-to-middle income country context), Australia and Germany.  
 - Identify key elements for implementation such as communication, documentation, education and policy. 
 - Reflect on how these insights can inform local practice and support a European framework.

Speakers:

Dr Caleb Gage, Paramedic, University of Cape Town, South Africa, 
Dr Eva Diehl-Wiesenecker, Consultant Emergency Medicine, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany; Department of Palliative Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, University of Augsburg, Germany
Ms Georgina Murphy-Jones, Deputy Director of Clinical Assessment and Pathways at London Ambulance Service, UK
Dr Martin Loucka, Founder, Center for Palliative Care, Czech Republic
Ms Michala Chatrna, Project manager and researcher, Center for Palliative Care & Masaryk University, Brno, Czech Republic
All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Care & Emergency Medical Services

description:
Session One. 
Wordcraft: Optimising writing for publication
This session will consist of two main elements: 
1.          All the World’s a Stage: Academic Writing for an International Audience
2.          Mad About Methods: Writing a Well-Crafted Methods SectionAim: To equip participants with some of the skills and knowledge needed to successfully publish research in palliative care journals. 
Learning objectives:

 Learning how to write for a global audience by using clear,      accessible language and framing research in a broadly relevant context;
 Developing the ability to construct transparent and rigorous      methods and ethics sections aligned with reporting standards.

By the end of this interactive session, participants will be better prepared to navigate the publication process and enhance the clarity, credibility, and impact of their palliative care research.
This session brings together three editors from the EAPC journals: Catherine Walshe and Sandra Martins Pereira from Palliative Medicine, and Christopher Jones from the Journal of Palliative Medicine. Together, they will share all you ever wanted to know about how to get your work published. Two interlinked and interactive sessions (this session today, and a second session tomorrow)  will focus on some of the most important aspects to ensure your work goes out for peer review (writing for your international audience and persuading the reader of the robustness of your methods and ethics procedures), and then, tomorrow,  how to respond appropriately to the peer review comments. If you have ever wanted to really understand how editors make their decisions on your research papers – these are the sessions for you.

title: EAPC Partnered Research
description:
Chairs: Cathy Payne (EAPC) and Minna Hokka (NursEduPal), Cathy Payne
Panel 5: Optimising Networks: From networks of expertise (NoEs) and clusters into future ways of working and collaborating
Networks of Expertise (NoEs) generate valuable evidence, tools, and collaborations in palliative care, but translating these outputs into enduring change remains a challenge. This panel will explore how network findings can move beyond publications to shape routine practice, policy, training, and ongoing professional collaboration. Panellists will discuss what elements should be sustained after NoEs conclude, and how professional organisations such as the EAPC can lead efforts to standardise approaches, support scale-up, and embed network outputs into everyday palliative care practice across Europe.
Panellists: Stein Kaasa ( JANE2), Cinzia Brunelli (EUonQOL and QOL Cluster), Carlos Centeno (EAPC Atlas), Erna Michiels (Hope4Kids), Phil Larkin (CODE-YAA)

title: TS: Innovative methods for implementation of digital tools in palliative care: insights from the 4D-PICTURE project
description:
Research into the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital tools in Palliative Care.

Increasingly, digital tools are developed to enhance the quality, accessibility, and coordination of care for persons with serious, life-limiting illnesses. While some tools are promising, few (less than 15%!) are sustainably adopted in practice. Key reasons are that such tools: a) lack a system approach, b) lack decent stakeholder collaboration; and c) are insufficiently integrated in complex, diverse care paths.   In the seven-country EU/UKRI funded 4D PICTURE project (2022-2027), we design, evaluate and implement digital decision-support tools in oncology and palliative care, and develop innovative methods to improve their implementation (https://4dpicture.eu/). This transdisciplinary project spans palliative care, public health, design, implementation science and many more disciplines. In this theme session, we demonstrate our ongoing work, and use prognostic tools and communication tools as case studies. We provide recommendations for the applicability of the three methods in diverse European palliative care settings. 
Introduction: Judith Rietjens, professor Design for Public Health.

Aims and learning objectives:To demonstrate three promising methods to improve the implementation of digital tools in palliative care:

1.	The digital NASSS implementation framework, to analyse the complexity of digital tools in seven domains and provide solution pathways to improve them;

2.	The Remote Participatory Bodystorming method, to gather stakeholder feedback on digital tools throughout their developmental process;

3.	The service design method MetroMapping, to visualise and redesign care paths to allow seamless integration of digital tools. 

After the session, participants have a clear understanding of the three methods. They leave with hands-on inspiration on how to use them across diverse palliative care settings.

title: EAPC Partnered Research
description:
Chairs: Carla Reigada (EAPC) and Maite Carrillo (PAINLESS)
Presentations: The Future of EU Funding Calls
This session will examine the new EU health research funding landscape, including mission-oriented approaches, public–private partnerships, widening participation mechanisms, and increasing emphasis on digital transformation, resilience, and implementation impact. The session will explore how the palliative care community can strategically position itself within future EU agendas to secure sustainable investment and strengthen its contribution to European health policy and systems innovation.
Presenters: Andreja Zulin de Swarte (EU Liaison officer, UMCU), Dirk Hadrich (EU Cancer Mission)

Panel 6: Engaging with policy
This panel will explore how research consortia can strategically engage policymakers at EU, national and regional levels through timely evidence synthesis, policy briefs, stakeholder alliances, and alignment with legislative and funding cycles. The session will highlight practical approaches to ensure palliative care evidence informs sustainable policy development across Europe.
Panellists: Nancy Preston (Pal-Cycles, EU PAL-COPD and PalSed), Tadeusz Hawrot (PsyPal), Tania Pastrana (RAPHAEL), Claudia Bausewein (VR TALKS) Alexandra Eni (ECO), Cinzia Brunelli (EUonQOL)

title: EAPC Groups: Global Caregiving in Focus: An Interactive Session to Guide Research, Health Systems, and Policy
description:
Designed to foster dialogue and collaboration, this interactive session hosted by the EAPC Reference Group for Family Caregiving aims to advance and prioritise the international research and policy agenda for family caregiving. 

The aims and learning objectives:
The aim of this interactive session is to provide an overview of new and emerging innovations in family caregiving and engage delegates in identifying priorities for advancing this field of research. The learning objectives are to: 
1. Educate attendees on new and emerging concepts and innovations in family caregiving, including global policy, technology innovations and research approaches. 
2. Facilitate audience engagement to actively co-produce ranked research priorities and capture stakeholder views to inform health policy and practice. 

Speakers: 
Prof Clare Gardiner, Professor of Palliative Care, UK 
Dr Viktoria Wallin - Marie Cederschiöld University, Sweden 
Prof Aline De Vleminck, Associate Professor at the End-of-life Care Research Group, Free University of Brussels (VUB) and Ghent University, Belgium

All speakers are members of the EAPC Reference Group for Family Carers.

TS: Researching new horizons for integrated, community-oriented health systems
description:
Research into Primary Care.

This dynamic and participatory session builds on recent global discussions and research around community-oriented primary palliative care, highlighting as care shifts to community settings, integration of palliative care within primary care is more essential.  The first presentation will share new international data on compassionate community interventions and outcomes. The second will explore implementation and evaluation of interventions in primary palliative care, focusing on equity, continuity, and measurable outcomes. The final speaker will present an emerging conceptual definition of primary palliative care as a bridge across systems, communities, and care providers. An interactive segment will follow, inviting delegates to co-create components of a shared definition using tools such as digital boards and word clouds. This collaborative process aims to advance a more inclusive and globally resonant framework for primary palliative care, aligned with WHO’s vision for universal health coverage. The session brings together researchers and practitioners from across continents and disciplines.

Aims and learning objectives:

This session explores innovative pathways to integrate palliative care within primary health systems, emphasising community-oriented care, measurable outcomes, and global equity. Participants will:

•	Examine global data and indicators essential for evaluating compassionate community models.

•	Reflect how palliative care can best be recognised, valued, and measured in primary care 

•	Understand a broader conceptualisation of primary palliative care

•	Engage in proposing a new research and policy agenda that integrates community capacity, informal networks, and lay caregiving into mainstream palliative care strategies and indicators

title: EAPC Groups: Palliative Sedation. Evidence, guidelines, and controversies
description:
Palliative sedation involves the intentional lowering of the level of consciousness in patients with life-limiting disease who are experiencing refractory suffering. There are many differences between European countries in its application and its use across palliative care practices. The session will start with explaining the main content of the updated framework on palliative sedation (published 2024), including some controversies. The session will continue with the main findings from a recent international multicenter study on palliative sedation (published 2024), showing a significant decrease of discomfort levels. The session will continue with experiences of relatives and healthcare professionals regarding palliative sedation (published 2025). Here, palliative sedation will be discussed as a complex intervention, with mixed experiences of relief and distress. Finally, the role of communication. Despite variations between settings, open dialogue with patients, families, and HCPs was considered valuable (publication 2025). The session will finish with space for discussion.
Attendees will learn which elements around palliative sedation reached expert consensus and which elements are still controversial in the debate surrounding palliative sedation, based on the updated framework for palliative sedation (published in 2024). In addition, highlights from European research will be shown regarding its medical aspects and the experiences of professionals and relatives. There will be space for a guided discussion.
Speakers:

Prof Dr Jeroen Hasselaar, Radboudumc, the Netherlands 

Prof Dr Sheila Payne, Lancaster University, England

Dr Daniel Balazs Fulop, Department of Primary Health Care, University of Pecs Medical School, Pecs, Hungary

All speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Sedation.

title: TS: Integrating palliative care into respiratory care: Challenges, innovations, and European collaboration
description:
Research into the management of symptoms and patient and family needs.

This themed session will feature three interconnected presentations.

Ágnes Csikós (University of Pécs) will discuss the challenges of integrating palliative care into respiratory care, including barriers at the patient, provider, and system levels, highlighting complexities such as unpredictable disease trajectories and the management of breathlessness.

Nancy Preston (Lancaster University) will present the ICLEAR intervention developed by Dr Paul Marsden at the Royal Preston Hospital in the UK, which helped integrate palliative care and improved communication between teams, reduced hospital admissions and enabled people to spend more time at home toward the end of life.

Julie Stevens (Vrije Universiteit Brussel) will introduce the EU PAL-COPD project, a large-scale, stepped-wedge RCT adapting and scaling the ICLEAR intervention across Europe. We will share preliminary findings from the first control wedge.

The session will conclude with a panel discussion inviting audience questions and reflections on the speakers’ experiences implementing ICLEAR in their respective countries.

Aims and learning objectives:

This session will highlight the importance of integrating palliative care into respiratory services for patients with advanced respiratory diseases. Participants will: Recognise the challenges and barriers to effective integration; Learn from the practical experiences of a UK study embedding palliative care within respiratory clinics; Gain insights into the EU PAL-COPD project, a European initiative focused on integrated palliative care in COPD. By the end of the session, attendees will be able to critically assess implementation strategies and explore ways to improve patient-centred care in respiratory services across diverse healthcare settings.

title: EAPC Groups: Strong Foundations, Shaky Grounds: LGBT+ Palliative Care in a Polarized World
description:
This session focuses on the implementation of the EAPC’s LGBT+ palliative care guidelines across varying cultural and geopolitical contexts. Katherine Bristowe will outline current translation and adaptation efforts across Europe. Theodor Kruse will address the urgent and specific needs of trans communities under threat, highlighting the role of palliative care professionals in responding to crisis with advocacy and action. Max Kleijberg will ground the discussion in real-world examples from Sweden, exploring practical tools for healthcare teams to offer inclusive care. Claude Chidiac will illustrate the adaptation of the guidelines in Lebanon, alongside related initiatives, highlighting the importance of community-led, partnership-driven responses within a socio-politically challenging context. Together, these presentations offer insight into translating policy into practice, building intersectional care structures, and responding to an increasingly polarized world.

This session aims to explore how EAPC recommendations for LGBT+ inclusive palliative care are being translated into local contexts amid rising anti-LGBT+ sentiment. Participants will learn how to implement culturally sensitive and inclusive practices, especially for trans individuals facing systemic threats. The session also fosters critical reflection on the intersection of care, politics, and equity, offering practical tools and solidarity-driven frameworks for clinical, educational, and policy responses.

Speakers:

Dr Katherine Bristowe – King’s College London, UK

Theodor P. Kruse – Sygehus Lillebælt, Denmark

Max Kleijberg – Mälardalen University / Karolinska Institutet, Sweden

Claude Chidiac – Homerton Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, UK / Lebanese Medical Association for Sexual Health, LebanonAll speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Palliative Care for LGBT+ People

TS: Emerging challenges in opioid prescribing for people with cancer
description:
Research into Public Health in Palliative Care.The global cancer burden is growing, with projected 35.3 million new cases worldwide by 2050. Opioids remain the cornerstone of management for cancer-related symptoms, such as pain, dyspnea, and cough. As more people live with cancer, opioid use in this population warrants critical reexamination—particularly in the context of the ongoing opioid overdose epidemic. Yet access to these essential medications remains profoundly unequal: some high-income countries face a crisis of opioid overuse and associated harms, while most of the world’s population has little or no access to opioid analgesia.

This session will explore emerging issues in opioid prescribing for people with cancer, including stewardship strategies for those with comorbid opioid use disorder or elevated risk of overdose, and the global impact of diversion and restrictive regulation on access in low-, middle-, and high-income countries. Participants will be invited to discuss how to balance opioid safety with compassionate, equitable access worldwide.

Aims and learning objectives:
1. Describe the evolving role of opioids in cancer care amid the dual global crises of opioid excess in some settings and restricted access in others

2. Identify strategies for opioid stewardship in cancer care, including for those with opioid use disorder or elevated risk of opioid overdose

3. Describe the methods of opioid diversion, gaps in the opioid supply chain, and ways of addressing these gaps

4. Assess the impact of restrictive laws and regulations on opioid access for people with cancer in low-, middle-, and high-income countries

title: EAPC Groups: Current scientific advances in pediatric palliative care: challenging care settings, perinatal palliative care and sedation
description:
This session will showcase current scientific developments in pediatric palliative care through three focused presentations. 

Creative Strategic Commissioning: Case studies from Austria and Ghana will illustrate innovative models for delivering care in resource-constrained settings, including interdisciplinary approaches, system-wide collaboration, and global action plans.
Perinatal Palliative Care: Speakers will explore the evolution of services across Europe, including antenatal planning, memory-making, and bereavement care. Novel research from Belgium, co-produced with bereaved families, will be presented alongside practical examples of personalized care and interdisciplinary collaboration.
Pediatric Palliative Sedation: Drawing on the first international survey of 348 physicians across five European countries, this segment will examine variations in indications, medication use, and ethical reasoning. The Dutch national guideline, currently the only evidence-based pediatric sedation framework, will be highlighted for its development and implementation.
The session concludes with a discussion on cross-country learning and strategies to improve equity and quality of care.
Aims and learning objectives:
This session aims to present cutting-edge research and practice developments in pediatric palliative care across Europe. Participants will gain insights into:

Innovative strategies for commissioning and delivering children’s palliative care services in resource-constrained settings, including interdisciplinary models and global action plans 

Advances in perinatal palliative care, including antenatal planning, memory-making, and bereavement support for families 

Evidence-based approaches to pediatric palliative sedation, highlighting international survey findings, medication use, and ethical frameworks

Attendees will learn how cultural, societal, and systemic factors shape care and explore practical solutions for improving quality and equity in pediatric palliative care, and will foster cross-country dialogue. 

Speakers:
Dr Jennifer Brandt – Paediatric Intensive Care Physician, University of Vienna (Austria) 

Prof Julia Downing – Chief Executive Officer, International Children’s Palliative Care Network (International) 

Dr Laure Dombrecht – Postdoctoral Researcher, End-of-Life Care Research Group, Vrije Universiteit Brussel & Ghent University (Belgium) 

Dr. Erna Michiels – Pediatric Oncologist, Princess Máxima Center for Pediatric Oncology (Netherlands) Pre-Recorded video presentation.

All speakers are members of the Children and Young People’s (CYP) Reference Group.

title: EAPC Groups: Patient-Centred Care in the Dying Phase: from Symptoms to Systems
description:
There are several key challenges to the adequate management of symptoms and needs in the dying phase, including limited education of healthcare professionals in palliative care and emotional discomfort with dying; fragmentation of care and poor communication among care teams, patients, and families; system pressure reducing the time available for holistic, patient-centred care; and misunderstandings about cultural or spiritual needs. In this session, we will discuss the following topics: 

Findings on the prevalence of symptoms and needs of dying patients and their families from the iLIVE project, an 11-country cohort study among 1400 patients in the last phase and life and their families. 

Experiences with a mobile application providing real-time access to patient information, enabling multidisciplinary collaboration in care for dying patients.  

Several examples of how benchmarking can be used in care of the dying, including the potential for international benchmarking.
Multidimensional management of needs in the dying phase is essential for ensuring a dignified and compassionate end-of-life experience for patients and their families. This approach addresses not only physical symptoms but also emotional, psychological, social, and spiritual needs. In this session, we want to discuss the prevalence of symptoms and needs of dying patients across different settings and patient groups; the use of technology in assessing and monitoring symptoms in the dying phase;  and how benchmarking can contribute to optimal management of symptoms and needs. 

Speakers:Prof Agnes van der Heide, Erasmus MC, The Netherlands
Dr Pilar Barnestein Fonseca, Cudeca Institute, Spain
Dr Antoine Pierre Michel Elyn, University Hospital of IcelandAll speakers are members of the EAPC Task Force on Care for the Dying in collaboration with the International Collaborative of Best Care for the Dying person
